title: The Algorithm of the Ballot: How Data Decides Democracy Before We Vote
content:
Elections used to be loud. Street-corner rallies, hoarse loudspeakers, campaigners going door to door, entire neighbourhoods gathered around a television for the evening debate. That version of democracy is dying, and most of us haven’t quite noticed the funeral. The real contest now happens somewhere quieter — inside a smartphone screen, in the space between a thumb and a feed. Political persuasion doesn’t shout at crowds anymore. It whispers to individuals, one at a time, and the whisper has been tested, refined, and timed with a precision no rally could ever match.

This isn’t speculation about some AI-run future. It’s already part of how political communication works in India and elsewhere with widespread mobile internet access.

Campaigns describe their own methods as “smart” and “surgical,” and for once the marketing language is accurate. Nobody is addressing an anonymous mass anymore. Every voter is a profile being built in real time — every scroll, every pause, every like or skip can become another data point feeding a model of who you are and what might move you. Linger two seconds longer on a video about unemployment, and your feed may begin showing you more content like it, each one worded slightly differently, until what started as manufactured content starts to feel like your own settled opinion.

title: Caste Denied, Gender Dismissed: Reading Literature, Love and Social Life through Selective Lenses
content:
Literature both reflects and shapes social life. This article examines how literature, people’s perspectives, and social life are deeply entangled. It asks how literary works and social relations are interpreted through selective lenses that foreground some forms of inequality while obscuring others. What readers notice in a literary work is not always separate from how they understand the social world around them. Their interpretations are shaped by what they recognise as important, what they have experienced, and what they may have learned to overlook. In this sense, reading is not simply an individual act of interpretation; it can also reveal how social inequalities are recognised, denied, or made invisible. Caste is denied in the name of progress and demanded in the name of awareness, while gender is dismissed in the name of unity. Through reflection on a poem and everyday experiences, this article shows how caste and patriarchy are intertwined rather than operating separately. Ignoring this reality reveals how easily we refuse to confront forms of inequality that do not directly affect us.

author: rti_admin
title: From Inheritance to Inquiry: The Courage to Question
content:
A society becomes dynamic not when everyone thinks alike, but when people possess the freedom and courage to question, debate and rethink what they have inherited. Every generation receives beliefs, customs, institutions and social practices from the past. Some enrich human life; others may perpetuate inequality simply because they have acquired the authority of tradition. The true measure of a mature society, therefore, is not how faithfully it preserves its inheritance, but how intelligently it examines it. In the Indian context, this becomes particularly important when we reflect upon caste, religion and patriarchy. These are not merely abstract concepts. They influence family life, marriage, social status, personal choices and opportunities. Yet meaningful discussion of them is often displaced by sentiment, identity politics, unquestioned authority or fear of disagreement. What India needs is not less tradition or less faith, but more reasoned discourse about their social consequences.

I. Caste, Religion and Patriarchy: Examining the Inherited Order

Caste is one of the most enduring forms of social stratification in India. author: rti_admin
title: AI for Humanity: A Buddhist Ethical Framework for the Age of Artificial Intelligence
content:
Artificial Intelligence is rapidly becoming one of the most transformative technologies in human history. In a remarkably short period, AI has moved from a specialised computational technology to a general-purpose tool capable of writing, designing, analysing, reasoning, generating images and video, assisting scientific research, and increasingly performing tasks once considered uniquely human.

This extraordinary development has produced two contrasting visions of the future. One imagines AI ushering in an age of unprecedented abundance, where machines perform much of the world’s intellectual and physical labour and humanity is liberated from scarcity. The other warns that increasingly autonomous and powerful AI systems could become difficult to control and, in an extreme scenario, pose an existential threat to humanity.

Both possibilities deserve serious consideration.

The crucial question, therefore, is not simply how intelligent AI can become, but what values will guide that intelligence.

Intelligence without wisdom can become dangerous. Power without character can become destructive. Knowledge without compassion can become indifferent to human suffering. And technological progress without concern for society’s welfare can increase inequality rather than reduce it.

title: Bablai Mata Yatra: How Does Development Politics Affect Madia Culture?
content:
For the Madia Adivasi community in the Bhamragad region, the Bablai Mata Yatra (pilgrimage/fair) is not just a religious pilgrimage but a living symbol of cultural, environmental, and constitutional rights.

However, in recent times, the politics of development, religious conversion, the administration, and Naxalism have begun to significantly impact the Bablai Yatra.

For the Madia Adivasi community in the Bhamragad area, the Bablai Mata Yatra is not merely a religious fair but a living symbol of their cultural, environmental, and constitutional rights. Every year, thousands of Madia Adivasi people from the Bhamragad tract come together to worship Bablai Mata and to renew their generations-old culture, traditions, and relationship with nature. Yet, in the name of development, the pilgrimage of Bablai Devi is slowly disappearing.

According to Adivasi tradition, Bablai was the sister of a man named Morka. Bablai was married to Thakur Dev, who is still worshipped at a shrine on Surjagad today. After their marriage, Thakur Dev went to Surjagad for a second wife, but Bablai did not go away with her people. She stayed in this region, remained among the people here, and became one with this land and forest.

The locals say that their faith was born from this sacrifice:
